stem: Which of the following best illustrates the value of episodic memory for 'recalling precedent'?

options.text: An agent generating random, unrelated text with no connection to any past situation
An agent reciting a general, timeless mathematical fact
An agent recalling how a similar past dispute was resolved to inform how it approaches a new, similar dispute
An agent refusing to recall anything from any past interaction

explanation.why_correct: Recalling how a similar past situation was resolved, to inform handling of a new similar situation, is exactly the 'recalling precedent' value that episodic memory provides.

why_incorrect.B: A timeless, general mathematical fact is semantic memory, not an example of recalling a specific past precedent.
why_incorrect.D: Refusing to recall anything is the opposite of using episodic memory to inform current reasoning.
why_incorrect.A: Random, unrelated text generation has no connection to recalling any specific relevant past situation.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Recalling precedent -- how a similar past situation was handled -- is a direct, practical application of episodic memory.

stem: What is the main efficiency benefit of maintaining procedural memory for recurring task types?

options.text: Guaranteeing that every future task of that type will be completed instantly with zero effort
Avoiding the need to re-derive a successful approach from scratch each time a similar task recurs
Eliminating the need for the agent to ever reason about anything again
Making all other memory types unnecessary

explanation.why_correct: Procedural memory's main efficiency benefit is avoiding the need to re-derive a known-good approach from scratch every time a similar task type comes up again.

why_incorrect.C: Procedural memory doesn't eliminate reasoning entirely; it provides a useful starting point or framework that may still require some reasoning to apply correctly.
why_incorrect.D: Procedural memory serves a distinct purpose from episodic and semantic memory; it doesn't make the others unnecessary.
why_incorrect.A: Having a stored procedure doesn't guarantee instant, zero-effort completion; some execution and reasoning is typically still required to apply it to the current specific case.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Procedural memory's core benefit is avoiding re-derivation of a known-good approach for recurring task types, not eliminating all further reasoning.

stem: Which statement correctly reflects the relationship between episodic and semantic memory as suggested by the generalization process?

options.text: They are distinct in function but can be connected -- semantic memory can emerge from patterns generalized across episodic observations
They are entirely unrelated with absolutely no possible connection of any kind
Episodic memory is just semantic memory with a different name
Semantic memory can never be influenced by episodic observations

explanation.why_correct: While episodic and semantic memory serve different functional roles, they are connected in that semantic memory can emerge from generalizing a recurring pattern observed across multiple episodic memories.

why_incorrect.B: There is a documented connection -- generalization from episodic observations into semantic facts -- so they are not entirely unrelated.
why_incorrect.C: They are distinct concepts with different defining traits (specific event vs. general fact), not simply different names for the same thing.
why_incorrect.D: Semantic memory can indeed be influenced by and generalized from a pattern across multiple episodic observations.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Episodic and semantic memory are functionally distinct but connected -- semantic facts can emerge by generalizing from recurring episodic patterns.

stem: Which of the following questions does semantic memory primarily help answer?

options.text: What is generally true, independent of any specific event
What exactly happened during a specific past conversation
How to execute a multi-step process
What is the agent's current session ID

explanation.why_correct: Semantic memory's defining role is holding general facts and knowledge that are true independent of any one specific event.

why_incorrect.B: What exactly happened during a specific past conversation is the defining question for episodic memory, not semantic.
why_incorrect.C: How to execute a multi-step process is the defining question for procedural memory, not semantic.
why_incorrect.D: A session ID is an unrelated technical/implementation detail, not connected to this memory-type distinction.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Semantic memory answers 'what's generally true' -- distinct from episodic ('what happened') and procedural ('how to do it').

stem: A help-desk agent needs to decide, for a new ticket, whether to: (1) recall how a similar ticket was resolved before, (2) look up the company's standing policy relevant to the ticket, or (3) apply a known, reusable triage procedure. Which memory types correspond to these three needs, respectively?

options.text: Episodic, semantic, procedural
Procedural, episodic, semantic
Semantic, procedural, episodic
All three needs correspond to exactly the same single memory type

explanation.why_correct: Recalling a similar past ticket is episodic (specific past event), looking up standing policy is semantic (general fact), and applying a known triage procedure is procedural (reusable method) -- in that exact order matching the three listed needs.

why_incorrect.B: This reorders the mapping incorrectly; recalling a similar past ticket is episodic, not procedural, and so on for the other two.
why_incorrect.C: This also misassigns the mapping; looking up standing policy is semantic, not procedural, and so on.
why_incorrect.D: These three needs are distinctly different in kind (specific precedent, general fact, reusable method) and map to three different memory types, not one single type.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Specific precedent recall = episodic; general policy lookup = semantic; reusable procedure application = procedural.

stem: Why is it inaccurate to claim that distinguishing episodic, semantic, and procedural memory implies these three types are completely unrelated to each other?

options.text: Because there is actually no distinction between any of the three types at all
Because the distinction is a design/organization tool for retrieval, and semantic memory can still be generalized from patterns in episodic memory
Because procedural memory is identical to semantic memory in every respect
Because episodic memory can never inform any other type of memory

explanation.why_correct: The three-way distinction is primarily a tool for organizing storage and retrieval around different functional needs, and this is compatible with the types being connected -- for example, semantic facts emerging from a generalized pattern across episodic memories.

why_incorrect.C: Procedural and semantic memory are functionally distinct (methods/sequences vs. general facts), not identical.
why_incorrect.D: Episodic memory specifically CAN inform semantic memory through generalization, contradicting this claim.
why_incorrect.A: There is a real, meaningful functional distinction between the three types, even though they can be connected.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: The episodic/semantic/procedural distinction organizes memory by function; it doesn't preclude connections like semantic facts emerging from episodic generalization.

stem: Which scenario best illustrates procedural memory being appropriately refined over time, rather than treated as fixed?

options.text: A stored triage procedure is updated after observing that a revised step order consistently produces better outcomes
A stored triage procedure is used exactly as originally written forever, regardless of its actual performance
A stored triage procedure is deleted the moment it is created, before ever being used
A stored triage procedure is converted into an episodic memory with no further use as a procedure

explanation.why_correct: Updating a stored procedure after observing it can be improved, based on evidence of better outcomes with a revised approach, is exactly the appropriate refinement behavior procedural memory is meant to support.

why_incorrect.B: Keeping a procedure fixed forever regardless of actual performance is the opposite of appropriate refinement.
why_incorrect.C: Deleting it before ever being used provides no opportunity to observe or refine its performance at all.
why_incorrect.D: Converting it to episodic memory removes its reusable, procedural function rather than refining it as a procedure.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Appropriately refining procedural memory means updating it based on observed performance, not keeping it rigidly fixed or discarding it entirely.

stem: A travel-booking agent wants to recall 'what special requests did this specific traveler make on their last three trips.' Which memory type is most directly relevant to answering this?

options.text: Procedural memory, since it concerns how to book a flight
Semantic memory, since it concerns a general fact with no connection to any specific trip
Episodic memory, since it concerns specific past trips and their specific details
No memory type is relevant to this request

explanation.why_correct: Recalling specific requests from specific past trips is exactly what episodic memory is designed to capture -- events tied to particular occasions, not general facts or procedures.

why_incorrect.B: This request is specifically about particular past trips, not a general, event-independent fact, so semantic memory isn't the primary fit.
why_incorrect.D: This is a direct, clear use case for episodic memory retrieval.
why_incorrect.A: The request concerns recalling what happened on specific past trips, not a method for performing the booking process itself.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Recalling specific details tied to particular past occasions is the core use case for episodic memory.

stem: Which pair correctly distinguishes semantic memory from procedural memory?

options.text: Semantic memory and procedural memory can only ever be used by entirely separate, unrelated agents
Semantic memory holds methods or sequences of steps; procedural memory holds general facts
Both are exactly identical with no distinguishable difference
Semantic memory holds general facts; procedural memory holds methods or sequences of steps for accomplishing tasks

explanation.why_correct: Semantic memory is specifically about general facts/knowledge, while procedural memory is specifically about methods or sequences for accomplishing tasks -- this is the correct distinction.

why_incorrect.B: This reverses the actual roles of the two memory types.
why_incorrect.C: They are clearly distinguishable: facts versus methods/procedures.
why_incorrect.A: Both memory types can coexist and be used together within a single agent; there's no requirement for separate agents.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Semantic memory = general facts; procedural memory = methods/sequences for accomplishing tasks.
